thread.title: Apple: The Smartphone Market's Competitive State - Apple AAPL)

author: Paulo Santos
title: Apple: The Smartphone Market's Competitive State - Apple AAPL)
text:
In the past, I wrote on how Android would catch up to Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) in terms of camera abilities . I also wrote on how smartphones would get good enough and ultimately get very low entry points for fully usable smartphones.
This article today will cover the competitive state of the market from a consumer’s perspective. This state is important, as it will ultimately determine the attractiveness for a consumer to choose the iPhone over a number of alternatives. The iPhone, of course, is and remains Apple’s most important product by far.
First, an important but well-known distinction:
Apple iPhones are the only smartphones able to run iOS . iOS is a closed ecosystem, and Apple controls all apps available on its iTunes app store. Jailbreaking to get access to apps not vetted by Apple or to have access to other possible app stores is a very difficult and rare process. All competitors run Android . Android is a free (to the manufacturer) and open-source operating system. Generally speaking, Android smartphones sold on markets outside of China will come pre-loaded with Google (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) apps as well as Google Play. Smartphones sold in China will come with Chinese app stores and not Google Play. Both inside and outside of China it’s possible to install an app store that’s different from Google Play. At all times, Android users can “sideload” apps from external sources with little difficulty (though this is often advised against, due to possible security threats). In the past, iOS was a very large advantage for Apple. There were simply more and better apps for iOS than for Android. That has long stopped being true. While arguably iOS might still have “better” apps (certainly when it comes to tablet apps), Android tends to have all the relevant apps. Indeed, Android has more apps in absolute terms, since Android dominates the smartphone market and is a clear leader in gigantic markets like China.
As a result of the above, as well as the widespread usage of Google’s ecosystem, it’s become easier and easier over time for smartphone users to switch back and forth between iOS and Android.
Finally, iOS, as a closed and less customizable system, tends to be easier to use and present fewer technical hassles. Android, as an open system, has more inconsistencies (it’s normal for smartphones to ship with lots of duplicate apps for the same purpose) and has long had more trouble when it came to operating system upgrades (though the upgrade problem is overstated, due to Android’s nature ).
Anyway, what matters today is that a smartphone buyer can rather easily compare Android smartphones and iPhones, and choose between them based on the experience he seeks, the features he wants and the price he's willing to pay.
Since Android is an open source operating system, it’s very hard for Android smartphone makers to differentiate themselves. This has led to an extremely competitive market, where new features spread like wildfire and margins are always compressed. As a result, Android smartphones tend to be cheap given what they deliver to the end user.
On Apple’s side, there has been an attempt over time to raise prices. This attempt is both driven by higher unit costs over time, as well as by trying to spruce up sales and profits in face of rather sluggish volume growth.
The combination of Android’s competitive struggle with Apple’s pursuit of higher prices has led us to the market which exists today. A market where the price differential between usable to excellent Android phones has become larger and larger versus the typical iPhone entry model. Let us thus check where things stand today.
The Entry-Level Market This represents the cheapest smartphones you can buy which will still be highly usable. Of note, there are even cheaper Android smartphones than those I’m going to highlight here, but those will already entail severe feature compromises, whereas these highlighted don’t.
A struggling entry-level smartphone
Some of the most amazing smartphones which can be bought at entry-level prices are LeEco variants. There are several related models, with minor specification differences between them.
For instance, a typical model, the LeEco Le2 x520, which can usually be bought under a promotion directly from China, costs under $90 .
For that price, the consumer gets (among other features):
A Qualcomm (NASDAQ: QCOM ) Snapdragon 652 CPU (4x ARM A72 big cores at 1.8GHz, 4x ARM A53 power saving cores at 1.2GHz). This CPU provides performance comparable to Android flagships from 2015. It’s perfectly usable without any performance issues. 1080p 5.5” high-quality LCD display. This provides image quality (if not color accuracy or display real estate) on a par with an Apple XR from today. 3GB RAM, 64GB storage. Same as an entry-level Apple XR today. 3,000 mAh battery. 16MP f/2.0 PDAF back camera, 8MP front camera. Both fully usable, producing mid-end images. A quick fingerprint reader. I call this a “struggling entry” because China is a strange market . The company manufacturing this phone, LeTV, has long been effectively bankrupt. This smartphone is likely being sold at or below cost.
There’s a downside, of course. Since the company can’t support the smartphone, its software has stagnated in time. This smartphone comes with Android 6.0, which will never see an update (outside of the consumer installing a custom ROM). It will still run all Android apps, and given Android’s nature, having an older OS doesn’t compromise the device’s functionality (but it might compromise its security at times). Still, this is a severe downside when Android is already up to version 9.0.
A typical entry-level smartphone
A more typical entry-level smartphone will be somewhat different. It will be supported by a viable manufacturer, but it will more closely reflect the underlying costs. However, it will also have a more up-to-date design and underlying software/operating system.
Here, I’ll provide as an example the Xiaomi Redmi 6 ( XI ). This is a phone which can easily be bought for $129.99 , while on frequent promotions.
For that price, the consumer gets:
A MediaTek Helio P22 CPU (8x ARM A53 cores at 2.0GHz). This CPU is visibly slower than that on the LeEco Le2, and corresponds roughly to an Android flagship from 2014. However, as it turns out, those flagships were the first perfectly usable Android flagship phones, whose usage wouldn’t disappoint a consumer from today. 720p 5.5” LCD display. This provides image quality slightly inferior to the previously presented LeEco, though still perfectly usable. 3GB RAM, 64GB storage. Same as an entry-level Apple XR today. 3,000 mAh battery. Double 12MP f/2.2+5MP back cameras. This allows for a decent, modern-looking bokeh effect on portrait photos. 5MP front camera. These cameras are fully usable, producing mid-end images. A quick fingerprint reader. Since this phone (and other comparable ones) is offered by a viable manufacturer (Xiaomi, in this case), its software is up to date, running an Android 8.1-based OS. The OS is now being updated to an Android 9.0-based OS.
As we can see, the entry-level smartphone market is now being served with fully usable smartphones which will run all Android software well enough and take decent photos. These phones are being offered in the $87-$130 range already. In terms of distribution, they’re mostly available through online channels, but brands like Xiaomi are now expanding physical distribution outside of China (not just into India, but also Europe).
The Mid-Range Market The mid-range smartphone market has also seen the effects of extreme competition. What the consumer gets going from the low-end market to the mid-range market are generally better specs when it comes to design, speed and camera quality.
Let’s see a typical offering at this level. I’ll use a Xiaomi offering here for several reasons:
It's typically available worldwide. It presents competitive pricing, though ultimately on a par with many other Chinese competitors which are less well-known in the West. Xiaomi’s policy regarding upgrading the OS, where other brands easily falter on their “lower than flagship” products. Here, I’ll focus on the Xiaomi Redmi Note 6 (which is about to be replaced by the Redmi Note 7, as Xiaomi product cycles are very quick). This is a phone which can easily be bought for $169.99 (32GB storage) to $209.99 (64GB storage).
For that price, the consumer gets:
A Qualcomm Snapdragon 636 CPU (4x Kryo 260 gold ARM A73 derivative cores at 1.8GHz, 4x Kryo 260 silver ARM A53 derivative power saving cores at 1.6GHz). This CPU provides performance close to that of a 2016 Android flagship. In usage, the consumer won’t feel any shortcomings. 1080p 6.26” 19:9 LCD display with a notch. This provides image quality which should be on a par with an iPhone XR, with slightly lower color accuracy. 3GB/4GB RAM, 32/64GB storage. 4,000 mAh battery. Double 12MP f/1.9 dual pixel PDAF+5MP f/2.2 back cameras. 20MP f/2.0 + 2MP f/2.2 front cameras. These cameras will provide near-flagship photos with good portrait modes on both sides (front and back). A quick fingerprint reader. As with other Xiaomi smartphones, the mid-range Redmi Note 6 has prospects for continued OS upgrades. Right now, it runs an Android 9.0-based OS.
The High-end Bargain Market This segment is comprised of smartphones that try to deliver the same specifications present on current Android flagships, at relative bargain prices. This is usually achieved by using components similar to those you expect to find on high-end flagships, but with the resulting smartphones being proposed by lesser-known brands at lower margins and, at times, slight compromises here and there.
The difference to the mid-range smartphones often appears in better displays, the highest-end CPUs and another step improvement in camera capabilities.
Here I’ll present 2 typical competitors (there are more). The $295.99 Xiaomi Pocophone F1 and the $397.99 Xiaomi Mi8. I could also include the OnePlus 6 as it fits the same segment and is often available near $400, however that’s not the case right now (they’re starting at ~$450 as I write this).
Here’s what the consumer gets with the Xiaomi Pocophone F1:
A Qualcomm Snapdragon 845 CPU (4x Kryo 385 gold ARM A75 derivative cores at 2.8GHz, 4x Kryo 385 silver ARM A55 derivative power saving cores at 1.7GHz). This is the same CPU powering nearly all 2018 Android flagships. In usage, the consumer will get the same performance as on other current Android flagships, no matter what the price. In some cases this can still trail the sheer power of an iPhone flagship, but not really to a noticeable extent. 1080p 6.18” 18:7 LCD display with a notch. This provides image quality which should be on a par with an iPhone XR, with perhaps slightly lower color accuracy. 6GB RAM, 64GB storage. 4,000 mAh battery. Double 12MP f/1.9 dual pixel PDAF+5MP f/2.2 back cameras. 20MP f/2.0 front camera. The main back camera is comparable to the one on the Xiaomi Mi8 minus OIS (Optical Stabilization). However, the secondary back camera is inferior (for depth sensing only, and not for telephoto use). Camera performance on the Pocophone F1 will thus fall between that of the Xiaomi Redmi Note 6 and that of the Xiaomi Mi8. A quick fingerprint reader. A more “plasticky” build, with a plastic back that’s already rare even on the low-end segment.
As for the Xiaomi Mi8:
A Qualcomm Snapdragon 845 CPU (4x Kryo 385 gold ARM A75 derivative cores at 2.8GHz, 4x Kryo 385 silver ARM A55 derivative power saving cores at 1.7GHz). This is the same CPU powering nearly all 2018 Android flagships. In usage, the consumer will get the same performance as on other current Android flagships, no matter what the price. In some cases this can still trail the sheer power of an iPhone flagship, but not really to a noticeable extent. 1080p 6.21” 18.7:9 AMOLED display with a notch. This provides image quality superior to that of an iPhone XR, and close to that of an iPhone X or XS, which also use OLED panels. 6GB RAM, 128GB storage. 3,400 mAh battery. Double 12MP f/1.9 dual pixel PDAF with OIS+12MP f/2.4 telephoto back cameras. 20MP f/2.0 front camera. Camera performance is close to other 2018 Android flagships, but not quite there yet. In typical usage, it will be hard to see a difference. A quick fingerprint reader. The main observation here is that flagship-level, or near flagship-level features are now available starting from $299-$399. The typical consumer would get similar satisfaction from these phones as he’d get from flagship Android phones as well as flagship iPhones, with minor nuisances here and there (such as the lack of OIS on the Pocophone).
The High-End Flagship Market Better-known brand names in the Android world still try for premium pricing. This is the case with Samsung, with the Samsung S9, or Huawei with the Mate 20, Mate 20 Pro and other models.
The Samsung ( OTC:SSNLF ) S9 can be gotten for $570 (64GB storage)/ $669 (128GB storage). Remember, list prices can be higher, but these are prices at which the phones can actually be bought new. The Huawei Mate 20 can be gotten for ~ $659 (128GB).
Here’s what the consumer gets with the Samsung S9:
A Qualcomm Snapdragon 845 CPU (4x Kryo 385 gold ARM A75 derivative cores at 2.8GHz, 4x Kryo 385 silver ARM A55 derivative power saving cores at 1.7GHz). 1440x2960 5.8” 18.5:9 AMOLED display. This resolution is higher than the other smartphones indicated here, but will typically run at 1080p. This provides image quality on a par with that of an iPhone XS, which also uses an OLED panel from Samsung. 4GB RAM, 64GB/128GB/256GB storage. 3,000 mAh battery. 12MP f/1.5-2.4 dual pixel PDAF with OIS back camera. 8MP f/1.7 front camera. Camera performance is near the top of 2018 Android flagships as well as on par with the iPhone. A quick fingerprint reader. IP68 water resistance.
As for the Huawei Mate 20:
A Huawei Kirin 980 CPU (2x ARM A76 cores at 2.6GHz, 2x ARM A76 cores at 1.92GHz, 4x ARM A55 cores at 1.8GHz). In practice, the Kirin 980 is the first next-generation CPU in the Android world. It will likely be surpassed by the Qualcomm Snapdragon 855 when it starts shipping in other well-known Android flagships in late February, early March. For now, the Kirin 980 is the closest in the Android world to the iPhone CPUs. This is so because it uses the new ARM A76 cores. 1080p 6.53” 18.7:9 LCD display with a very small notch. This provides image quality on a par or better than an iPhone XR, but short of the OLED iPhones (X, XS) as well as the Samsung S9 and even the mid-range Xiaomi Mi8. 4GB RAM, 128GB storage. 4,000 mAh battery. Triple back camera: 12MP, f/1.8, 27mm (wide); 16MP, f/2.2, 17mm (ultrawide); 8MP, f/2.4, 52mm (telephoto). 24MP f/2.0 front camera. Huawei is now conquering the top of the charts in terms of photo quality. DXOMark hasn’t reviewed the Mate 20 yet, but it’s likely that it will once again get very high marks. On the downside, the Mate 20 doesn’t include OIS in its main camera. A quick fingerprint reader. No water resistance. The high-end Android phones are typically comparable to high-end iPhones. This will be even more evident in 2019, as Apple's rather large single-thread CPU performance difference will narrow substantially then. That said, even now that difference isn’t readily apparent to the common user.
While list prices for well-known brands’ Android flagships are usually not very distant from the iPhone, in practice that isn’t the truth. iPhones aren’t available at significant discounts to list prices, while nearly all Android phones are. That applies to the highest end as well. As we saw here, the price point on these two examples was just $570-$659.
As for the iPhone, the entry list prices for the latest generation are:
$749 (iPhone XR 64GB); $999 (iPhone XS 64GB) and; $1,099 (iPhone XS Max 64GB). These list prices stand in stark contrast to the many examples of current Android smartphones.
Even if we use older generation iPhones, we have:
$449 (iPhone 7 32GB); $569 (iPhone 7 Plus 32GB); $599 (iPhone 8 64GB); $699 (iPhone 8 Plus 64GB). Those prices are closer to what’s available on Android world's “high-end bargains” and “high-end” bins, but they all carry outdated designs and lack features in several ways.
On China And Elsewhere All of this smartphone market analysis refers to the prices these phones can be gotten in the West. When it comes to China, an interesting thing happens:
Most of these phones can be had for even lower prices (possibly excluding the high-end Samsungs). The Apple iPhone prices are higher in China than in the US. They're also higher in USD when translated from European EUR prices. As a result, the differentials we see here are worse in practice for most of the world.
Another Problem When I was putting together the list, I also indicated that the lower-end and mid-range Android offerings were also matching the performance of 2015-2016 Android flagships. This has another implication, which is:
A 2015-2016 flagship, be it an Android smartphone or an iPhone, was already enough to satisfy most users’ current demands. Of course, the battery might die and need replacing. The RAM on the older iPhones was stingy. And so on. But the fact is, flagship-level 2015-2016 smartphones are perfectly usable today, as are mid-range phones from years in between, or low-end smartphones from today. This introduces maturity to the market. A lot of the demand will be dictated by the need to replace broken phones, but the need to get more usable phones is being significantly reduced.
This acts as a significant headwind for all smartphone makers, including Apple. This will only get worse, as consumers buying the low-, mid- or high-end today will likely all be satisfied for years, versus mostly high-end customers being satisfied for years with the prior iterations.
Conclusion Apple, in raising its entry prices for its latest iPhone generations, is creating a wider gap to fully usable Android smartphones at all levels. And this is happening at a time when even low-end Android phones are providing a decent experience from $85-$129 onwards.
It’s also happening when mid-range Android phones, from $170-$200, provide the experience of recent flagship Android phones. And even fully spec’d bargain Android flagships are now available at $299-$399.
This reality is likely to put continuous pressure on the iPhone sales volume. And given intense competition in the Android world, this reality is only set to worsen.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
